facts: Maui is the second-largest Hawaiian island, formed by two massive shield volcanoes joined together.
Haleakala, Maui's highest peak, is a dormant volcano standing over ten thousand feet above sea level.
The famous Road to Hana features over six hundred curves and fifty-nine bridges through lush tropical rainforests.
Humpback whales migrate to Maui's warm, shallow waters every winter to mate and give birth.
The island takes its name from the legendary Polynesian demigod Maui, who pulled the islands from the ocean.
Maui is famous for its vibrant poke, a fresh raw fish dish seasoned with sea salt and seaweed.
Lahaina was once the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom and a major global whaling port in the nineteenth century.
The Maui Marathon is one of the oldest marathon events in the western United States.
Ocean waters off Maui's coast boast world-class surf breaks like Peahi, famous for its massive winter waves.
Traditional Hawaiian lei are often crafted from sweet-smelling plumeria flowers growing abundantly across the island.
Maui is home to unique endangered species like the nene, the official state bird of Hawaii.
The Lahaina Banyan Tree, planted in 1873, grew to cover an entire city block.
Iao Valley State Park features an iconic needle-shaped peak surrounded by dense, emerald rainforest.
Traditional Hawaiian luau feasts celebrate island heritage with kalua pork cooked in underground ovens.
Maui's volcanic soil nurtures world-famous sweet onions known for their mild and juicy flavor.
Surfing pioneer Duke Kahanamoku often visited Maui, helping popularize the ancient royal sport worldwide.
Molokini Crater, located just off Maui's coast, is a crescent-shaped volcanic islet offering crystal-clear snorkeling.
High altitude on Haleakala creates one of the best locations in the world for optical astronomy.
Ancient Hawaiians built extensive stone pathways across Maui, some of which runners still trace today.
Hawaiian sugar cane plantations once dominated Maui's landscape for over a century before closing down.
